transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-21
Start time (UTC): 15:00
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Elena Park, Marco Ruiz, Tara Singh (Redwood) — James Hooper, Sana Malik, Liam O'Connor (Mistral Insurance)

Summary:
Redwood team walked through BYO HSM provisioning workflow, differences between cloud KMS and HSM attestation, and audit scope for upcoming SOC 2/ISO audit. Customer asked deep questions about key custody, key wrapping, rotation, and how Redwood handles model-serving keys in a private deployment. Action items and next steps captured.

Topics covered:
- BYO HSM onboarding workflow and connector options (KMIP, PKCS#11)
- HSM attestation and FIPS/FedRAMP vs customer policy
- Audit logs: what Redwood records, log format, retention and tamper-evidence
- RBAC & SSO integration (SAML/SCIM) for key ops and admin roles
- Key rotation, escrow, and emergency key-revocation processes
- Network/topology for Private deployment (VPC peering, egress controls)

Action items (quick list):
- Send HSM onboarding checklist and network diagram (Redwood)
- Customer to share approved HSM vendors and contract timeline (Mistral)
- Draft rotation/playbook for model-serving keys (Redwood SE)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Elena Park: All right, hey everyone thanks for carving out time. Uh this is Elena from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. With me, Marco our Solutions Engineer and Tara our security PM. How are you all doing?

[00:12] James Hooper: Doing well thanks. We wanted to use this session to—uh—talk through the BYO HSM process and make sure we can show auditors how keys are provisioned and rotated. We've got SOC 2 in Q1 so, timeline is tight.

[00:28] Marco Ruiz: Great, yeah Marco here. We'll start with high level then dive into the actual provisioning flow. Quick Q for you, James — are you leaning on managed HSMs from vendor or are you acquiring physical FIPS modules in-house?

[00:40] James Hooper: We have a mix. Procurement prefers managed HSM for speed — like CloudHSM — but compliance team wants hardware attestation evidence and sometimes a dedicated on-prem HSM for certain lines. So we might do a blen—blend of both.

[00:56] Sana Malik: And one thing — we need to ensure key material never leaves our control. BYOK is a must. We also have requirements around key rotation windows and multi-person approval for key export.

[01:10] Tara Singh: Right, thanks Sana. We'll show how Redwood's Private deployment can integrate with your KMS and support HSM-backed CMKs. We support KMIP and PKCS#11 connectors and have an HSM connector that does key-wrapping so the unwrapped key never touches the Redwood control plane.

[01:28] Liam O'Connor: Quick question on the wrapping — if we wrap a key with our HSM and send it to Redwood, what exactly is stored in Redwood? The wrapped blob only, or are there any derivatives?

[01:40] Marco Ruiz: Only the wrapped blob. In our Private mode, the runtime only stores the encrypted key material — we never have the plaintext key. During startup, a secure unlock happens in a short-lived enclave and the decryption keys remain in the HSM. There is also an option to cache a session key in RAM for performance but we can disable that if you need zero persistence.

[02:05] James Hooper: That helps. For auditors we need an attestation flow — chain of custody. How do you provide proof that key rotation happened and which operator initiated it?

[02:18] Tara Singh: We produce audit logs with a cryptographic hash of the event record and a timestamp. Logs include actor (SSO id), operation (rotate/export/import), key id, and before/after key version. We can export logs in JSON and ship to your SIEM — or you can point a log-forwarder to our pull endpoint.

[02:38] Sana Malik: Are those logs tamper-evident? Can they demonstrate non-repudiation?

[02:44] Marco Ruiz: We use append-only write-once log buckets with server-side signing. For Private deployments you can bring your own logging collector and we recommend streaming to your Splunk/ELK cluster. The signed digest is recorded in the event so you can validate integrity. It's not a full PKI timestamp authority but it meets typical SOC 2 attestation asks — we can provide a walkthrough of the signed log format.

[03:10] James Hooper: You mentioned SSO. We use SAML with SCIM provisioning, and need role separation between platform ops and key custodians. How granular is your RBAC?

[03:23] Elena Park: Good question. Our RBAC supports role-based policies + resource-level allow lists. For keys specifically we have a Key Admin, Key Operator, and Audit-only role. Key Admin can provision bindings, Key Operator can rotate but not export, and Audit-only is read-only for logs. We also integrate with your IdP for SAML SSO and SCIM for groups.

[03:45] Liam O'Connor: Does Redwood support MFA for key operations? We prefer enforced MFA for approve/export flows.

[03:52] Tara Singh: Yes — for any sensitive ops we support step-up auth via SAML assertion that triggers your IdP's MFA. We also support approval workflows where two operators must sign off (2-person control) using an approval policy.

[04:08] James Hooper: One of our auditors asked about key escrow and emergency rotation. If a key is compromised, what's the process to revoke and rewrap model-serving keys with minimal downtime?

[04:20] Marco Ruiz: We recommend a staged rotation: 1) create a new key and wrap it in your HSM, 2) register new key with Redwood, 3) drain old sessions, 4) flip traffic to the new key. For model-serving, we can do rolling restarts at the shard level so latency spikes are minimal. We also support automatic fallback to a secondary key (hot standby) if configured.

[04:45] Sana Malik: Does the rotation require model checkpoint rewrite or do you rotate the encryption at the transport layer?

[04:54] Marco Ruiz: It depends. For token-level KV caches we re-encrypt ephemeral caches; for persisted checkpoints we rewrap metadata references — rarely do we need a full checkpoint rewrite. We can provide a sample runbook that shows the exact sequence for your infra.

[05:12] James Hooper: Ok, can you also show evidence you support FIPS 140-2 / 140-3 validated modules? Our procurement wants to ensure the HSMs are validated.

[05:22] Tara Singh: Absolutely. We maintain a list of validated HSMs in our docs and we can include FIPS certificate numbers and attestations. For managed HSMs we map vendor certs and provide the relevant compliance pages.

[05:35] Elena Park: Quick aside — do you have a preference for network topology? Private deployment can be deployed in your VPC and we can do VPC peering or private link. Any egress restrictions?

[05:46] Liam O'Connor: All egress to public internet is blocked by default — only approved endpoints. We'll need an on-prem connector or AWS PrivateLink.

[05:56] Marco Ruiz: Good — PrivateLink is supported. We'll include an architecture diagram showing dataplane and control-plane endpoints.

[06:05] Sana Malik: A little detail — what about metrics and telemetry? We need to ensure telemetry doesn't include sensitive metadata or key ids in cleartext.

[06:14] Marco Ruiz: Telemetry is redacted by default. We send metrics like decrypt latency, error rates, and token counts but we hash identifiers and never transmit plaintext key material. We can show the telemetry schema.

[06:28] James Hooper: Can we talk about audit scope — exactly which events are considered 'crypto operations' in Redwood logs?

[06:36] Tara Singh: Sure, core crypto events are: key.create, key.import, key.rotate, key.export, key.revoke, decrypt.request, wrap/unwrap, and key.policy.change. Each event logs the user principal, IP, timestamp, and outcome.

[06:52] James Hooper: Do you retain logs for 7 years if needed? Our reg team asks for long-tail retention for some financial records.

[07:00] Marco Ruiz: Out of the box we offer 90 days retention for hosted. For Private customers you can configure retention to any policy you need — including cold-archive to S3 Glacier or on-prem tape via your pipeline. We'll show configuration options in the handbook.

[07:15] Sana Malik: Regarding key lifecycle policy enforcement — can we require minimum rotation cadence and deny manual rotation outside of schedule?

[07:23] Tara Singh: Yes, we have guardrails and policy enforcement. You can set required rotation cadence, maximum key age, and disallow manual exports unless the policy allows. Policies are enforced at the control plane.

[07:36] Liam O'Connor: For HSM onboarding, does Redwood provide a pre-built KMIP connector or do we need to build an adapter?

[07:45] Marco Ruiz: We have pre-built KMIP and PKCS#11 connectors for the major vendors and a lightweight adapter for custom vendors. For on-prem HSMs we can run a small connector as an appliance in your network that mediates all KMIP calls.

[07:59] James Hooper: On the encryption algorithm side, do you support RSA, AES-256-GCM, and AEAD for metadata? Also interested in post-quantum options for long-lived keys.

[08:10] Marco Ruiz: AES-256-GCM is our default for symmetric keys, and we support RSA-OAEP for asymmetric wraps. For PQ, we have an experimental module for hybrid key-wrapping (classical + PQ key-encrypt) — it's not GA yet but we can discuss timelines.

[08:30] Sana Malik: Can Redwood sign audit events with our own key so we can validate authenticity later?

[08:36] Tara Singh: Yes — you can provide an audit signing key (or Redwood can hold one in your HSM) and we will sign event batches. The verification key can be managed by you.

[08:50] James Hooper: Another auditor ask — separation of duties for key provisioning. We need to show that provisioning cannot be done by an individual that also has approval rights for exports. How do you enforce that?

[09:02] Marco Ruiz: That's enforced through RBAC + approval policies. Provisioning role and export approval role are distinct and mapped to IdP groups. We also emit policy enforcement events to the audit log so you can prove separation.

[09:18] Elena Park: I'm going to share my screen with the HSM onboarding checklist — quick callout the checklist includes network ports, certificate exchange, vendor certs, and attestation docs.

[09:28] Speaker 2: (screen shown) // some screen annotations, list items flicker.

[09:40] Marco Ruiz: I'll call out the certificate exchange step — we recommend an out-of-band transfer of the CSR/attestation and use a known PKI channel. Also note if you use a vendor's root certs we include them in the truststore.

[09:59] James Hooper: For the attestation report what level of granularity do you provide? Do you include nonce-based challenge response?

[10:08] Tara Singh: We support nonce-based attestation for compatible HSMs — the HSM will sign the nonce and we capture the attestation statement including firmware version, serial, and cert chain.

[10:20] Sana Malik: Ok, about disaster recovery — if an HSM site is lost, how do you orchestrate a failover without compromising keys?

[10:30] Marco Ruiz: We recommend dual-wrapped keys: primary HSM wraps the active key, and a secondary HSM wraps a backup copy. The system verifies attestation from secondary before failing over. DR tests are documented and we can help run tabletop exercises.

[10:48] James Hooper: One more procurement detail — licensing for dedicated Private deployment and whether there are extra fees for HSM connector.

[10:57] Elena Park: There is a connector support fee if we manage on-prem appliance, otherwise the connector code is open and runs in your environment with no additional license. We'll include pricing in the follow-up.

[11:10] Liam O'Connor: Are there any perf penalties we should expect with HSM-bound key ops? For low-latency inference we care about additional ms per token decrypt.

[11:22] Marco Ruiz: HSM ops add latency on unwrap calls. Typical unwrap is 5-20ms depending on the HSM and network. We mitigate with session key caching and local enclave to reduce per-token round trips. If you require absolute <5ms we can architect with local at-rest decryptors and ephemeral session keys under your policy.

[11:45] Sana Malik: Can you provide benchmark numbers for common HSM vendors?

[11:50] Marco Ruiz: Yes — we'll run a small benchmark with your expected sequence length and token rate. We'll need a test tenant and access to your HSM or a managed HSM instance.

[12:05] James Hooper: Ok let's talk about encryption-at-rest for model weights and embeddings — do you encrypt those with customer keys or Redwood-managed keys?

[12:16] Marco Ruiz: For Private deployments you can choose customer-managed keys (BYOK) for object storage encryption. For hosted mode we offer Redwood-managed keys but dedicated customers can request CMKs.

[12:30] James Hooper: Any special handling for embeddings since they're PII sensitive in our use case?

[12:36] Tara Singh: We recommend encrypting embeddings at rest with CMKs and also using tokenization or hashing before storage. We can add an extra layer of application-level encryption if needed.

[12:50] Elena Park: Quick note — we'll include a data flow diagram in the follow-up that highlights where keys are used for model weights vs ephemeral tokens.

[13:00] Sana Malik: Can Redwood generate an exportable compliance pack for auditors with sample evidence?

[13:06] Tara Singh: Yes, we produce a compliance bundle for customers containing SOC 2 attestation, ISO artifact mapping, and sample audit logs. For Private customers we can populate redacted evidence tied to your tenant.

[13:20] James Hooper: Do you have a runbook for incident response involving key compromise? We need to show we can rotate quickly and validate that no plaintext ever left.

[13:32] Marco Ruiz: We do — it covers containment, rotate/rollover, forensic artifacts, and postmortem. We also include hash-based evidence that plaintext didn't leave the runtime. We'll share the runbook.

[13:45] Liam O'Connor: There was an item about escrow — do you support third-party key escrow for long-term recovery?

[13:53] Tara Singh: We support escrow workflows and can integrate with your approved escrow provider. Escrow copies are split (Shamir-style) and require multi-party unwrap.

[14:05] James Hooper: Great. On the timeline, procurement wants the SOW and pricing by end of month — can you hit that?

[14:12] Elena Park: We can. We'll send draft SOW and preliminary pricing by 2026-11-26.

[14:20] Sana Malik: A small nit — how do you handle key identifiers in logs to avoid leaking tenant info?

[14:28] Marco Ruiz: Keys are assigned internal opaque IDs, we hash them before sending to hosted telemetry. For customer-owned log exports we can keep full ids in your internal log only.

[14:40] Speaker 3: // brief cross-talk about scheduling.

[14:48] Marco Ruiz: One more tech note — if you want HSM-on-prem with a connector appliance, the appliance will run in an isolated subnet and only allow KMIP calls from the Redwood runtime subnets. It's hardened and we provide the image and hardening checklist.

[15:06] James Hooper: Sounds good. Could you also include a sample audit query to show evidence of a rotate event for auditors?

[15:12] Tara Singh: We'll include sample queries for Splunk and Elastic including the exact fields and expected results.

[15:25] Elena Park: Let's capture next steps — I'll read them out: Redwood will send HSM onboarding checklist, architecture diagram, sample runbook for rotation and DR, pricing and SOW draft by 11/26. Marco will draft key rotation playbook by 11/24. Tara will export the audit-log retention matrix and RBAC mapping template by 11/23. Mistral will share approved HSM vendors list by 11/25 and confirm test tenant access for benchmarking.

[15:55] James Hooper: That aligns. We'll get procurement looped in and share vendor list.

[16:02] Sana Malik: Thanks everyone. Small follow-up — can we posture a short 2-hour workshop where we provision a dummy key and rotate it? Preferably next week.

[16:12] Elena Park: Yes we can do that. We'll propose a slot.

[16:18] Liam O'Connor: Thanks all.

[16:20] Elena Park: Thanks — we'll follow up with links.

[16:28] (meeting ends)
